summary: The root M-N-Y primarily signifies measuring, estimating, or determining something. It also relates to decreeing, appointing, or ordaining, often with a sense of predestination or fate.

provenance.lane: Edward William Lane, An Arabic-English Lexicon (1863-93), public domain. Digital text via Perseus, Tufts University, CC BY-SA 3.0 US.
provenance.summary: Editorial summary derived from the Lane entry. NOT Lane's own wording. Shown as a gloss only; the Lane text below is the source.

headwords.def: He tried him; proved him. (S, K.) You say, مَنَاهُ اللّٰهُ بِحُبِّهَا God tried him by love of her. (T.) And مُنِىَ بِكَ َا He was tried by such a thing. (T.) مَنَى He meditated [a thing in his mind]; syn. قَدَّرَ. (Bd, ii. 73.) See أَمِنْيَّةٌ.
He wished, or desired, it. (K, TA.) التَّمَنِّى relates to that which is possible and to that which is impossible: whereas التَّرَجِّى relates only to what is possible. (I'Ak, p. 90.)
said of a she-camel: see 8 in art. سمو.

A thing wished for by a man: pl. مُنًى. (T.) This word and signify the same. (M, Mgh, Msb, K.) See an ex. in a verse cited voce أَوْ المُنْيَةُ in the case of a covered she-camel, The period by the end of which one knows whether she be pregnant or not. (M.) مُنْيَةٌ of a mare, Twenty days. (M, voce سَفُودٌ.)

[ A decreed event. Fate; destiny: ] The decree of death: (IB:) or the decreed term [ of life, or] of a living being: (Er-Rághib:) death; (S, M, K;) because it is decreed; (S, M;) as also: (M, K:) [properly a thing decreed: and hence the pl.] المَنَايَا signifies the fates or decrees [ of God ]. (T.) مَنِيَّةٌ also means (assumed tropical:) A man of courage upon his saddle: (TA in art. حوى:) pl. مَنَايَا: see an ex. voce حَوِيَّةٌ.

An object of wish, or desire: originally, a thing that a man meditates ( يُقَدِّرُهُ ) in his mind; from مَنَى signifying قَدَّرَ: and hence applied to a lie; and to what is wished, or desired, and what is read, or desired [pl. أَمَانِىُّ and أَمَانٍ ]. (Bd in ii. 73.) See مُنْبَةٌ and حَجْوَى.

headword_note: Lane organises by verb form and principal noun, not by every inflected form. A word with no headword entry falls back to the root meaning; nothing is inferred.
